jZh9J0tkzl4.title: Tazkiyah Halaqa: Mortality, Episode 23
jZh9J0tkzl4.one_line: Mortality is a gift, not a curse: accepting that life ends makes every moment valuable, present and urgent.
jZh9J0tkzl4.summary: Continuing the mortality pillar of his tazkiyah series, he separates death, a single unknown moment that is always a loss because it ends the chance to improve, from mortality, the fact that we are finite, which he calls a gift from Allah. Accepting mortality begins with sadness and moves through the stages of grief, just as reality in marriage differs from what men imagine; holding onto the illusion causes misery, while accepting reality opens a better life. Finite things are valuable and infinite things are not, so limited time creates urgency and beauty. He offers a hypothesis that Allah places us in a finite world first so we can appreciate the eternal life He offers later, and supports the idea with novels about immortality that always reintroduce death. The Prophet lived fully in each moment because he valued it. He describes walking out alive from a Syrian detention facility in 2013 as the only survivor, and warns against the psychology of exempting ourselves from what befalls others. He asks the audience to stop hiding death in a blind spot, to count the visits left with aging parents, to drop the word 'later', and to be present in prayer and with loved ones.

outline.heading: Mortality as the pillar that holds tazkiyah together
outline.gist: Of the five pillars of tazkiyah, removing mortality or resurrection makes the whole equation collapse.

outline.heading: What the Quran says about death
outline.gist: Everything on earth perishes except Allah; death comes to you, it is what you tried to avoid, and every soul will taste it. Even the Prophet was told he would die.

outline.heading: Hadith on remembering death
outline.gist: The Prophet wept at a grave and told the companions to prepare; the smartest people remember death most and prepare for it, and remembering it in hardship eases it.

outline.heading: Death versus mortality
outline.gist: Death is an undefined moment and always a negative; mortality is the fact of being finite, and making peace with it is how you take death seriously.

outline.heading: Why death itself is a loss
outline.gist: At death the chance to repent, improve and draw closer to Allah ends, so you want life to end well, but mortality is the opposite of this loss.

outline.heading: Acceptance begins with grief
outline.gist: Accepting mortality brings sadness and the stages of denial, anger, bargaining and depression before acceptance, as with any gap between imagination and reality.

outline.heading: Example: marriage as imagined versus real
outline.gist: Men who insist marriage match the picture in their heads make themselves and their wives miserable; those who accept it as it is can enjoy it.

outline.heading: Our delusional view of mortality
outline.gist: We avoid the topic, so our view is delusional; accepting that every moment brings us closer to the end is sad at first but changes how we experience life.

outline.heading: Finitude creates urgency
outline.gist: If we were immortal nothing would ever need doing now; limited time that cannot be extended makes urgency the centre of existence.

outline.heading: Finite things are valuable
outline.gist: Infinite resources lose value; water and clean air became precious only once they seemed scarce.

outline.heading: Why Allah gave a finite life before eternity
outline.gist: His hypothesis: the worldly part of us cannot appreciate abundance, just as a child given everything becomes spoiled and unloved.

outline.heading: Time is the one thing you cannot buy
outline.gist: Gold, clothing and houses can be replaced but not time, and here rich and poor are equal.

outline.heading: Living finitely to appreciate Paradise
outline.gist: Eternal life offered to someone who never knew mortality would go unthanked, so we live a finite life first to value what Allah will give.

outline.heading: Hiding death in a blind spot
outline.gist: We watch people fall off the cliff daily, attend janazahs, then go back to not thinking about it to avoid sadness.

outline.heading: Choosing between illusion and truth
outline.gist: Either keep living through a corrupt lens or absorb the sadness and live life truthfully, which is far better on the other side.

outline.heading: The Prophet lived in the moment
outline.gist: He enjoyed life deeply and worried little about his own future, teaching that food for tonight and a place to sleep is enough.

outline.heading: Counting the visits left with aging parents
outline.gist: Seeing a parent monthly for ten years is only 120 visits; knowing the number makes each meeting more beautiful and worth enjoying.

outline.heading: Novels of immortality always bring death back
outline.gist: Every novel series imagining human immortality ends with mortality reintroduced, because existence without end has no meaning.

outline.heading: Every breath beautified
outline.gist: The best gift about your time is that it ends, so each breath, meeting and prayer gains value.

outline.heading: Midlife crisis as a crisis of delusion
outline.gist: People who ignored mortality hit a crisis when their bodies decline and often do something foolish they regret.

outline.heading: In a hundred years no one here will remain
outline.gist: A century is short; everyone in the room will be gone, and accepting this brings sadness first.

outline.heading: Acceptance brings peace and gratitude for being alive
outline.gist: Once the sadness sinks in, it brings peace and appreciation that you are still here to breathe, learn, hope and love.

outline.heading: The Prophet fully present with family
outline.gist: He played with his grandchildren for hours and was wholly with whoever he sat with, because he valued the moment.

outline.heading: Distraction in prayer
outline.gist: Waiting for salah or a session to end comes from not valuing the present; wandering thoughts are anxiety that achieves nothing.

outline.heading: Imagine it is your last
outline.gist: Treating a moment as your last intensifies living; the companions saw death often and needed few reminders.

outline.heading: Professional distance versus exempting yourself
outline.gist: Detachment is needed to serve patients, but applying it to your own mortality is a mistake.

outline.heading: Death is the only certainty
outline.gist: Nothing else in life is guaranteed; everyone here will be buried and forgotten within a week.

outline.heading: Lessons from near-death experiences
outline.gist: Survivors live better for a while, and keep that quality only if they keep contemplating their mortality.

outline.heading: His survival of a Syrian detention facility
outline.gist: He walked out alive in April 2013 as the only survivor; his priorities changed completely until the effect wore off years later, and he treats his life as extra time.

outline.heading: The psychology of exemption
outline.gist: We protect ourselves by assuming disasters seen elsewhere will not happen to us, to avoid feeling vulnerable.

outline.heading: Never say 'that would not be me'
outline.gist: Claiming you could never be the addict or the afflicted is arrogance; you control none of the variables, so praise Allah for where you are.

outline.heading: Mortality brings humility
outline.gist: Internalising mortality also brings humbleness and pragmatism to everyday life.

outline.heading: No more 'later'
outline.gist: Accepting mortality removes procrastination in your relationship with Allah, your deen and your loved ones, because 'later' banks on a certainty you lack.

outline.heading: What accepting mortality gives you
outline.gist: It beautifies and intensifies life, brings peace and motivation; time is the one thing you cannot get refunded, yet using it well includes sitting with tea and taking in beauty.

outline.heading: Mortality as a gift, to be argued further
outline.gist: Living the moment intensely and using time well is what mortality offers; he promises more arguments next week.

themes.note: Choose truthful acceptance over a comfortable illusion about death.

3:137.ar: قَدۡ خَلَتۡ مِن قَبۡلِكُمۡ سُنَنࣱ فَسِيرُواْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ فَٱنظُرُواْ كَيۡفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلۡمُكَذِّبِينَ
3:137.en: Systems have passed away before you. Do but travel in the land and see the nature of the consequence for those who did deny (the messengers)

3:138.ar: هَٰذَا بَيَانࣱ لِّلنَّاسِ وَهُدࣰ ى وَمَوۡعِظَةࣱ لِّلۡمُتَّقِينَ
3:138.en: This is a declaration for mankind, a guidance and an admonition unto those who ward off (evil)

3:139.ar: وَلَا تَهِنُواْ وَلَا تَحۡزَنُواْ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلۡأَعۡلَوۡنَ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ
3:139.en: Faint not nor grieve, for ye will overcome them if ye are (indeed) believers

3:140.ar: إِن يَمۡسَسۡكُمۡ قَرۡحࣱ فَقَدۡ مَسَّ ٱلۡقَوۡمَ قَرۡحࣱ مِّثۡلُهُۥۚ وَتِلۡكَ ٱلۡأَيَّامُ نُدَاوِلُهَا بَيۡنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلِيَعۡلَمَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَيَتَّخِذَ مِنكُمۡ شُهَدَآءَۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
3:140.en: If ye have received a blow, the (disbelieving) people have received a blow the like thereof. These are (only) the vicissitudes which We cause to follow one another for mankind, to the end that Allah may know those who believe and may choose witnesses from among you; and Allah loveth not wrong-doers

3:141.ar: وَلِيُمَحِّصَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَيَمۡحَقَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
3:141.en: And that Allah may prove those who believe, and may blight the disbelievers

3:142.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتُمۡ أَن تَدۡخُلُواْ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ وَلَمَّا يَعۡلَمِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ جَٰهَدُواْ مِنكُمۡ وَيَعۡلَمَ ٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ
3:142.en: Or deemed ye that ye would enter paradise while yet Allah knoweth not those of you who really strive, nor knoweth those (of you) who are steadfast

3:143.ar: وَلَقَدۡ كُنتُمۡ تَمَنَّوۡنَ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ مِن قَبۡلِ أَن تَلۡقَوۡهُ فَقَدۡ رَأَيۡتُمُوهُ وَأَنتُمۡ تَنظُرُونَ
3:143.en: And verily ye used to wish for death before ye met it (in the field). Now ye have seen it with your eyes

3:144.ar: وَمَا مُحَمَّدٌ إِلَّا رَسُولࣱ قَدۡ خَلَتۡ مِن قَبۡلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُۚ أَفَإِيْن مَّاتَ أَوۡ قُتِلَ ٱنقَلَبۡتُمۡ عَلَىٰٓ أَعۡقَٰبِكُمۡۚ وَمَن يَنقَلِبۡ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيۡهِ فَلَن يَضُرَّ ٱللَّهَ شَيۡـࣰٔ اۚ وَسَيَجۡزِي ٱللَّهُ ٱلشَّٰكِرِينَ
3:144.en: Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him. Will it be that, when he dieth or is slain, ye will turn back on your heels? He who turneth back on his heels doth no hurt to Allah, and Allah will reward the thankful

3:145.ar: وَمَا كَانَ لِنَفۡسٍ أَن تَمُوتَ إِلَّا بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِ كِتَٰبࣰ ا مُّؤَجَّلࣰ اۗ وَمَن يُرِدۡ ثَوَابَ ٱلدُّنۡيَا نُؤۡتِهِۦ مِنۡهَا وَمَن يُرِدۡ ثَوَابَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ نُؤۡتِهِۦ مِنۡهَاۚ وَسَنَجۡزِي ٱلشَّٰكِرِينَ
3:145.en: No soul can ever die except by Allah's leave and at a term appointed. Whoso desireth the reward of the world, We bestow on him thereof; and whoso desireth the reward of the Hereafter, We bestow on him thereof. We shall reward the thankful

t2eKdM7hg38.speaker_note: His own tafsir series; speaks as the centre's imam mourning one of its founders who taught Quran behind the scenes and resisted his attempts to honour him.
t2eKdM7hg38.title: Listening to the Divine: Aal-Imran 137-145
t2eKdM7hg38.one_line: The post-Uhud verses on loss: history repeats, the days alternate, do not weaken, and the deen does not die with any man.
t2eKdM7hg38.summary: A khutbah in his Listening to the Divine series on Aal-Imran 137-145, the verses revealed after the defeat at Uhud, delivered the week a founder of the centre, a Quran teacher who shunned the spotlight, passed away. He begins with the series' premise: the Quran is Allah's first communication to you, so you listen and then answer. The sunan of 3:137 are the patterns of history, not the Prophet's sunnah: defeat has happened before, so travel the earth and stop treating your story as unique. Do not weaken or grieve; the wound you took the enemy took too, and the days alternate so that nobody wins or loses every time. He warns against saying everyone has luck except you, since what is bad could get worse and ingratitude costs you what you have. Uhud was a felt defeat whatever strategists say; the Prophet went home missing people and visited the martyrs every week until he died. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, who lost everything for Islam and died with a cloth too short to cover him, is the example of a believer purified by trial. The second khutbah on 3:143-145 insists the deen is not tied to any man: when a prophet, scholar or teacher dies the work continues, every soul has its appointed time, and nothing is forever.

outline.heading: Opening
Recitation of the passage
outline.gist: He recites Aal-Imran 137 to 145, from the patterns that have passed before you to the reward of the grateful.

outline.heading: The Quran as Allah's first word to you
outline.gist: We hear verses through habitual interpretations, but the Quran is Allah's initial communication, after creating us, addressed to the Prophet's generation and to you specifically.

outline.heading: A relationship is not one-sided
outline.gist: If you speak to Allah all the time and feel no answer, remember He initiated the conversation long ago; He spoke first and you speak back, or a gap opens between you and Him.

outline.heading: Uhud: the losses behind these verses
outline.gist: The verses came after Uhud, where the Prophet was wounded and Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib, Mus'ab ibn Umayr and others were killed, leaving the companions shaken and questioning.

outline.heading: A loss in the community
outline.gist: One of the centre's pioneers, who taught Quran behind the scenes and worked to avoid any recognition, has died. Loss leaves bitterness and reminds us of the day we will not be here, and no verses address it more clearly than these.

outline.heading: Sunan: the patterns of history
outline.gist: Sunan here does not mean the Prophet's sunnah or its fiqh but the recurring patterns that have passed before you: defeat has happened many times before.

outline.heading: Travel the earth: your story is not unique
outline.gist: We get stuck in our own bubble and think our story matters uniquely; look at the end of those who denied, even if they enjoyed a moment on the mountain top. This is a clarification for people and guidance for the God-conscious.

outline.heading: Do not weaken, do not grieve
outline.gist: Do not let weakness, humiliation or sadness over a setback ruin your morale, make you ashamed of who you are or stop you moving forward; you are the superior ones if you believe.

outline.heading: The same wound touched them
outline.gist: If a wound touched you, one like it touched the enemy. Addressed to the companions but living on for everyone: will you let this cost you hope, momentum, grit and resilience?

outline.heading: Remember Badr: the days alternate
outline.gist: When you went home on top of the world after defeating the strongest army in the region, they took the wound. The days rotate among people: no one nails it every time and no one fails every time.

outline.heading: Beware saying everyone has luck but me
outline.gist: What is not going well could always go worse; lose the ability to be grateful and you may lose what you later realise was beautiful. Allah is speaking to His Prophet, so who am I to ask why He does not give me more?

outline.heading: Uhud was a defeat
outline.gist: Whatever the military explanations, the companions walked away feeling defeated and Quraysh went home feeling victorious. The Prophet went home missing people and visited the martyrs' graves every week until he died, greeting Hamza, Mus'ab and Anas ibn an-Nadr.

outline.heading: Did you think you would win every battle?
outline.gist: Losing momentum and hope after one hard day assumes you would win every battle to the end; one day you are up and one day you are down, and this is said to the Prophet himself.

outline.heading: That Allah may know the believers and take martyrs
outline.gist: The days alternate so that Allah makes known who truly believes and takes martyrs from among you; trials are an exam that exposes people.

outline.heading: Mus'ab ibn Umayr's short shroud
outline.gist: A man of twenty-six or so who lost everything for Islam from the day his mother threw him out, never married, never saw a victory and left nothing; his one cloth could not cover both head and feet, and the companions wept.

outline.heading: Purified, and exposed by hardship
outline.gist: Mus'ab became their example. Allah purifies the believers and destroys the disbelievers; did you think you would enter Jannah before He knew who strove and who was patient? Hardship exposes people; what did you think would happen?

outline.heading: Interlude
You wished for death, then saw it
outline.gist: They had said bring on the battle, we will fight and die, and then they saw death with their own eyes. When the Prophet was said to be killed, some went back and some stayed.

outline.heading: Muhammad is only a messenger
outline.gist: If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Every man, however great, will die; is your relationship with Allah tied to a person?

outline.heading: The work does not stop when a teacher dies
outline.gist: You carry this deen because you believe in Allah, whoever is around. When we lose a scholar or a teacher the work continues, or what was the point? Abu Bakr reminded them at the Prophet's death that Allah is alive and does not die.

outline.heading: No soul dies before its time
outline.gist: Turning back harms Allah nothing, and He rewards the grateful. Every soul dies by His permission at a set term; fifty years from now no one in this room will be here. Nothing is forever, especially not us.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.note: Setbacks are part of the recurring pattern of history and of every life; do not let them weaken or humiliate you, since the days alternate and Allah uses hardship to distinguish and purify the believers.

themes.label: Mortality, death and preparing for it
themes.note: Everyone dies at an appointed time; in fifty years nobody in the room will remain, so live the time you have in a way that earns a good ending.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: Mus'ab ibn Umayr gave up wealth, family and comfort from the day his mother threw him out, never saw a victory, and died at Uhud with nothing; the companions wept over his short shroud and he became their example.

themes.label: Patience (sabr) and perseverance
themes.note: Do not weaken and do not grieve: a difficulty must not cost you hope, momentum, grit or perseverance; you are the superior ones if you believe.

themes.label: Istiqamah: incorruptibility, steadfastness, moral integrity
themes.note: Do not turn back on your heels when a leader dies; carry the deen because you believe in Allah, not because of who is around, and keep the work going when teachers pass.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: Be careful of complaining that everyone has luck but you; what is not going well could go worse, and losing gratitude can lose you blessings you only recognize later.

themes.label: Relationship with the Quran: reading, reflecting, living it
themes.note: The Quran is Allah's first communication to you; read it as His side of a two-way relationship rather than through habitual interpretations.

themes.label: Islamic history and civilization
themes.note: Sunan are the laws of history that repeat; travel the earth and see the outcomes of those who denied before you.

hadith.gist: The Prophet kept visiting the martyrs of Uhud until he died, greeting them: peace be upon you, abode of believing people; peace be upon you Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib, Mus'ab ibn Umayr, Anas ibn an-Nadr.
Mus'ab ibn Umayr was killed at Uhud leaving only one cloth; when it covered his head his feet showed and when it covered his feet his head showed, and the companions wept.
At the Prophet's death Abu Bakr reminded the people that Allah is alive and does not die, and recited that Muhammad is only a messenger.

Xx3t5lMYJl8.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Qiyamah, Part 2: Verses 7-19
Xx3t5lMYJl8.one_line: Scenes of the Day with nowhere to flee, and the core of the passage: every human has full insight into himself and should stop self-deception.
Xx3t5lMYJl8.summary: The sheikh explains why Al-Qiyamah addresses the mind before the heart: emotions are the most valuable and vulnerable part of a person, so reason must clear the ground before the heart is invested, in faith as in marriage. After recapping the oaths, he moves through the scenes of the Day: eyes stunned as if by lightning, the moon eclipsed, sun and moon brought together, and man asking where to flee. Unlike any earthly disaster, there is no shelter and no cover; every road ends before Allah, the final residence. Man is told what he sent ahead and what he held back, yet verses 14 and 15 reach the heart of the passage: the human being is insight upon himself, even when he offers excuses. Children lie when no one can prove otherwise, adults perfect the habit, and some will even swear falsely to Allah. He urges honesty with others, and at the very least with oneself, citing the man whose ninety-nine scrolls of sin were outweighed by one card because he argued nothing. He reads verses 16-19 two ways: as guidance to the Prophet on receiving revelation, or as words to a person hurrying past the shameful parts of his own book. When people deny, their own limbs testify, so tap into that insight now.

outline.heading: A surah that speaks to the intellect
outline.gist: He takes Al-Qiyamah slowly because its dawah challenges logic and purpose rather than greed or fear, unlike the two surahs that follow it.

outline.heading: Move greed and fear one step past death
outline.gist: Humans are naturally greedy and scared of the future; no one is faulted for that, as long as both emotions reach beyond this life.

outline.heading: The mind governs the heart
outline.gist: Following the heart blindly almost always ends in regret. The deen stimulates the intellect first, then invests the heart fully; emotions built on a lie collapse violently.

outline.heading: Your heart is what you have of most value
outline.gist: Money is the cheapest thing you can give, time is worth more, and your love and passion are the most valuable and vulnerable. Opening it to everyone without thought sets you up for scars.

outline.heading: Marriage paves the ground for the heart
outline.gist: Marriage makes sure the right questions are asked, often by experienced people, before you fall in love. Islam is where your heart belongs fully, but make sure the reasoning is right first.

outline.heading: Withdrawn love does not return the same
outline.gist: Pulling back love leaves the heart hesitant and weaker, so reason comes first; the surah's first oath is by the conscience that questions every choice.

outline.heading: Recitation from verse seven
outline.gist: He recites to the end of the page, promising to read it all with translation later.

outline.heading: Stopping on a doubled letter
outline.gist: A tajweed note: stopping on a letter with shaddah requires emphasizing it; such verse endings are rare in the Quran.

outline.heading: Recap: the two oaths and man's excuse
outline.gist: Allah swears by the Day He takes a stand on each person and by the conscience that knows the right answer whatever Google says. Man's real problem is wanting a guilt-free life of sin.

outline.heading: When is this Day? Is there time?
outline.gist: Wanting to sin, man asks when the Day will be, hoping he still has time to do his thing.

outline.heading: Eyes stunned as if by lightning
outline.gist: Many Quranic scenes describe the onlooker rather than the event. Bariqa comes from lightning: eyes fixed and dilated by a sight never seen before.

outline.heading: The moon eclipsed, sun and moon joined
outline.gist: Khusuf is the dimming of the moon; the cosmos collapses in on itself and the sun crashes into the moon.

outline.heading: Looking for a safe place in a disaster
outline.gist: In tornadoes, earthquakes or fires we want to gather our family, drive away and find shelter, even an underground bunker.

outline.heading: Nowhere to run when the universe collapses
outline.gist: Mountains crumble, valleys fill and seas burn, and everyone is driven to one place, exposed. Man asks where the escape is.

outline.heading: No refuge, no cover
outline.gist: Allah Himself answers: no wazar. The root means a cover, which is why sin (wizr) is so called, as it covers the heart and good deeds.

outline.heading: Al-mustaqarr: the final residence
outline.gist: Everything in this world is temporary. The only place to run to is your Lord, where you settle for good.

outline.heading: All roads lead back to Allah
outline.gist: Whatever path you take, you are marching toward Him and will find yourself standing before Him.

outline.heading: The surah that speaks to every insan
outline.gist: No surah uses the word insan as often, even the long ones; the experience is universal regardless of race, religion, age or sex.

outline.heading: Informed of what he sent ahead and held back
outline.gist: Man is told what moved him closer to Allah and what pulled him back, or what he did early and late in life. A hadith qudsi: it is only your deeds that I count for you.

outline.heading: Our existence is that simple
outline.gist: A few laps around the sun and we are gone; one meteor erases every trace. We over-complicate it: you return to Allah, the good and bad are shown and added up.

outline.heading: Another bal: the real problem
outline.gist: There is nowhere to run. Every bal in the surah signals that what came before is not the real issue.

outline.heading: Basirah: insight, not eyesight
outline.gist: The real issue is that man has full insight into his intentions, emotions and choices. It is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests.

outline.heading: Man is insight upon himself
outline.gist: First doubt about the bones, then the wish for guilt-free sin, and finally the truth: he is insight upon himself, yet lies to himself and others to avoid changing.

outline.heading: We hate being told we were the problem
outline.gist: We avoid answers that demand different choices and find it painful to hear that we caused a failure.

outline.heading: A generation that cannot take feedback
outline.gist: Criticism now comes sandwiched, and people collapse into years of therapy when told plainly they did it wrong; he wonders how we will survive that.

outline.heading: Children lie when no one can prove it
outline.gist: A child who was not seen defends a false story because his parents cannot prove otherwise, equating unprovable with untrue.

outline.heading: Your parents know because they were you
outline.gist: Parents know the real motive because they once did the same thing, though they will not admit it.

outline.heading: Adults perfect the habit
outline.gist: Left unchecked, the habit grows until nothing is admitted unless caught red-handed, and even then the narrative is shaped to look less malicious.

outline.heading: Swearing falsely to Allah
outline.gist: Some will swear to Allah on that Day as they swear to people, having lied so long they no longer know what is true.

outline.heading: The good news: you have insight
outline.gist: You can see your faults, accept blame and improve. Some people come to him with no insight at all, ignoring their share of the blame.

outline.heading: Hearing the holes in their story
outline.gist: When someone cannot see the blame their own account reveals, he ends the meeting, because they have chosen to lie to themselves.

outline.heading: Even if he offers his excuses
outline.gist: People cannot see through you, but Allah will lay everything open, however many excuses about being tired or overworked are thrown out.

outline.heading: At least admit it to yourself
outline.gist: If you cannot admit fault to others, say it to yourself: my intention was bad, I was negligent, I knew what I was doing.

outline.heading: Blankets over the radio
outline.gist: Self-deception is smothering a radio that keeps telling you the truth. He is not licensing lying to people; honesty with all is best, but never fail to be honest with yourself.

outline.heading: Deep inside you know He is there
outline.gist: Whatever an atheist argues, insight tells you that you were never alone, that He gave you much and expects something, and that responsibility means change.

outline.heading: Not lying to Allah will save you
outline.gist: However many mistakes and lies to others, keeping that inner honesty brings the humility that will serve you when you come to Him.

outline.heading: The man with ninety-nine scrolls
outline.gist: A man's sins tower on his scale like the Burj Khalifa. Asked whether the recording angels wronged him or he has an excuse, he says no: that was me.

outline.heading: The card that outweighs everything
outline.gist: Called back with the match seemingly lost, he is given a card bearing the testimony of faith; it sends the scrolls flying, for nothing outweighs Allah's name.

outline.heading: They argued nothing
outline.gist: The killer of many and others in the sunnah who were forgiven share one trait: they sat quietly and admitted everything.

outline.heading: I have nothing to say but Your mercy
outline.gist: We all sin, but meeting Allah ashamed, with nothing to defend yourself with after His blessings, is powerful; the alternative is a cooked narrative of parents, school and hardship.

outline.heading: Excuses beat tired parents, not Allah
outline.gist: A child with fifty excuses outlasts a tired mother or a father home after ten hours of work; that skill will not work with Allah.

outline.heading: Advice to the young: do not master self-deception
outline.gist: As an older brother he urges young people to strengthen their conscience and insight, accept accountability for each mistake and grow into better adults. He recites the last verses.

outline.heading: First reading: the Prophet and revelation
outline.gist: A common view takes verses 16-19 as an aside to the Prophet: do not rush your tongue to memorize; Allah will gather, recite and explain it. He accepts it as correct.

outline.heading: Second reading: the one reading his own book
outline.gist: He prefers the view that fits the flow: on the Day a person reading his record hurries past the embarrassing parts and is told not to rush.

outline.heading: Slow down: We will explain why you did it
outline.gist: Allah compiled the book and will have it recited slowly, then clarify every act and its motive; you speed because you know the fault is yours.

outline.heading: Repent while defence is still possible
outline.gist: In this world you found a way around your faults; there, nothing defends you. Acknowledge and repent now and Allah will forgive.

outline.heading: Your own limbs will testify
outline.gist: Those who have shut down their insight will deny, so Allah makes their tongues, hands, feet and skin speak against them.

outline.heading: Tap into your insight
outline.gist: The surah's dawah speaks to the part of you that knows the truth and that He is there. Use it instead of fighting or fleeing it, and live with more peace.

3:169.ar: وَلَا تَحۡسَبَنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ قُتِلُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمۡوَٰتَۢاۚ بَلۡ أَحۡيَآءٌ عِندَ رَبِّهِمۡ يُرۡزَقُونَ
3:169.en: Think not of those, who are slain in the way of Allah, as dead. Nay, they are living. With their Lord they have provision

3:170.ar: فَرِحِينَ بِمَآ ءَاتَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضۡلِهِۦ وَيَسۡتَبۡشِرُونَ بِٱلَّذِينَ لَمۡ يَلۡحَقُواْ بِهِم مِّنۡ خَلۡفِهِمۡ أَلَّا خَوۡفٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحۡزَنُونَ
3:170.en: Jubilant (are they) because of that which Allah hath bestowed upon them of His bounty, rejoicing for the sake of those who have not joined them but are left behind: That there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve

3:171.ar: ۞يَسۡتَبۡشِرُونَ بِنِعۡمَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَفَضۡلࣲ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُضِيعُ أَجۡرَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
3:171.en: They rejoice because of favour from Allah and kindness, and that Allah wasteth not the wage of the believers

3:172.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ٱسۡتَجَابُواْ لِلَّهِ وَٱلرَّسُولِ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مَآ أَصَابَهُمُ ٱلۡقَرۡحُۚ لِلَّذِينَ أَحۡسَنُواْ مِنۡهُمۡ وَٱتَّقَوۡاْ أَجۡرٌ عَظِيمٌ
3:172.en: As for those who heard the call of Allah and His messenger after the harm befell them (in the fight); for such of them as do right and ward off (evil), there is great reward

3:173.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ قَالَ لَهُمُ ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّ ٱلنَّاسَ قَدۡ جَمَعُواْ لَكُمۡ فَٱخۡشَوۡهُمۡ فَزَادَهُمۡ إِيمَٰنࣰ ا وَقَالُواْ حَسۡبُنَا ٱللَّهُ وَنِعۡمَ ٱلۡوَكِيلُ
3:173.en: Those unto whom men said: Lo! the people have gathered against you, therefor fear them. (The threat of danger) but increased the faith of them and they cried: Allah is Sufficient for us! Most Excellent is He in Whom we trust

3:174.ar: فَٱنقَلَبُواْ بِنِعۡمَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَفَضۡلࣲ لَّمۡ يَمۡسَسۡهُمۡ سُوٓءࣱ وَٱتَّبَعُواْ رِضۡوَٰنَ ٱللَّهِۗ وَٱللَّهُ ذُو فَضۡلٍ عَظِيمٍ
3:174.en: So they returned with grace and favour from Allah, and no harm touched them. They followed the good pleasure of Allah, and Allah is of Infinite Bounty

3:175.ar: إِنَّمَا ذَٰلِكُمُ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ يُخَوِّفُ أَوۡلِيَآءَهُۥ فَلَا تَخَافُوهُمۡ وَخَافُونِ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ
3:175.en: It is only the devil who would make (men) fear his partisans. Fear them not; fear Me, if ye are true believers

2:154.ar: وَلَا تَقُولُواْ لِمَن يُقۡتَلُ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمۡوَٰتُۢۚ بَلۡ أَحۡيَآءࣱ وَلَٰكِن لَّا تَشۡعُرُونَ

fUTGHrT0c5o.title: Post-Fajr Quranic Story: The Martyrs of Uhud and Hamra al-Asad
fUTGHrT0c5o.one_line: The story behind Al Imran 3:169-175: Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram's martyrdom at Uhud and the wounded companions who marched to Hamra al-Asad saying 'Allah is sufficient for us'.
fUTGHrT0c5o.summary: He explains a passage from the part of Al Imran that deals with Uhud, arguing that its treatment of the psychological and social aftermath of defeat matters for Muslims today, especially in the West. After reciting 3:169-175 he tells the story of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram, one of the leaders chosen at the second pledge of Aqabah and father of Jabir: his eagerness for martyrdom, his dream of a companion killed at Badr who said Allah had brought them to life in Jannah, his death at Uhud, and the Prophet's consolation to the weeping Jabir that Allah spoke to his father face to face and that the verse 'do not think those killed are dead' came down in answer to his wish. He explains the life of the barzakh as real but transitional. He then turns to the day after Uhud, when the Prophet marched the wounded to Hamra al-Asad to stop enemies from growing bold, and Abu Sufyan paid riders to spread fear. Their answer, 'Allah is sufficient for us', the words of Ibrahim in the fire, shows that true faith grows with hardship while hypocrisy breaks under it, and that Shaytan only frightens through his own allies.

outline.heading: Opening
Why the Uhud verses matter today
outline.gist: The verses on Uhud in the second half of Al Imran address the personal, psychological and social challenges after a defeat, which Muslims in this era and in the West need to understand well.

outline.heading: Recitation of the passage
outline.gist: He recites the verses on the martyrs being alive with their Lord and on those who answered the call after being wounded.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram at the second pledge of Aqabah
outline.gist: He introduces Abdullah, father of Jabir, among the seventy who pledged at the second Aqabah and one of the leaders chosen there.

outline.heading: Father and son both want to go out
outline.gist: An elderly father and his son both prepared to fight, and the father told the son that one of them must stay behind.

outline.heading: "If it were anything but Jannah"
outline.gist: Settling who would go, the father said he would have given way to his son in anything except Jannah, and expected to be martyred.

outline.heading: The dream: did you not die at Badr?
outline.gist: Abdullah saw a companion killed at Badr who said Allah had given them life and they fly in Jannah wherever they wish, and that Abdullah would soon join them.

outline.heading: Jabir weeps for his father
outline.gist: After Uhud Jabir hid his face crying, and told the Prophet his father had died leaving him nine daughters to care for.

outline.heading: Allah spoke to him face to face
outline.gist: The angels shaded him with their wings, and Allah spoke to him without a veil and invited his wish; he asked to return and be killed again, and when told none return, asked that those behind be told, so the verse was revealed.

outline.heading: Do not think, do not say: they are not dead
outline.gist: He compares the two verses that forbid calling the martyrs dead and even assuming it, because they enjoy a real form of life.

outline.heading: The barzakh: a transitional life
outline.gist: The barzakh is a place between places with some consciousness but not full life until resurrection; for martyrs the change is small, as they continue in joy and provision with their Lord.

outline.heading: Rejoicing and good news for those behind
outline.gist: The martyrs rejoice in Allah's bounty and give glad tidings about those yet to join them, who will have no fear or grief.

outline.heading: After Uhud: enemies grow bold
outline.gist: Tribes broke treaties and the treacherous killings of Muslims followed because the defeat made Muslims look weak, so the Prophet acted to reduce that threat.

outline.heading: The call to march to Hamra al-Asad
outline.gist: The day after Uhud the Prophet called out whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day to go out with him, allowing only those who fought at Uhud.

outline.heading: The wounded carry one another
outline.gist: Wounded companions carried each other to answer the call; Jabir, who had been excused from Uhud, was allowed to come.

outline.heading: Ma'bad al-Khuza'i warns Abu Sufyan
outline.gist: Ma'bad told Abu Sufyan that Muhammad had come out with companions burning to fight, which turned the Quraysh away from returning.

outline.heading: Abu Sufyan pays riders to spread fear
outline.gist: Abu Sufyan paid a passing caravan in food to tell the Muslims that a huge army had gathered against them.

outline.heading: "People have gathered against you": faith increases
outline.gist: Those who answered despite wounds heard the paid warning and it only increased their faith.

outline.heading: The same response at the Confederates
outline.gist: When the believers saw ten thousand Confederates they said this is what Allah and His Messenger promised, and it only increased their faith and submission.

outline.heading: Hardship deepens true faith; hypocrisy breaks
outline.gist: The greater the challenge, the deeper real faith roots itself; hypocrisy can survive small difficulties but any large one shakes it loose.

outline.heading: Hasbuna Allah: the words of Ibrahim in the fire
outline.gist: Ibn Abbas said Ibrahim spoke these words when thrown into the fire and the companions spoke them when told people had gathered against them.

outline.heading: What 'sufficient' means
outline.gist: Hasb means enough: with Allah you need nothing more and no one else.

outline.heading: They returned with grace, untouched by harm
outline.gist: They came back from Hamra al-Asad with Allah's favour and no harm, having followed His pleasure.

outline.heading: Shaytan frightens through his allies
outline.gist: Shaytan knows who is on his side and uses them to plant fear, but a true believer fears only Allah.

outline.heading: Outro

dZgChp01WTk.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Qiyamah, Part 3: Verses 20-40
dZgChp01WTk.one_line: The surah's final passage: love of the immediate, faces that see their Lord, the soul at the collarbones, and the closing question of purpose.
dZgChp01WTk.summary: Completing the surah, the sheikh first explains why dawah must engage the mind before emotion, having seen many young Canadian Muslims lose their faith when that order was reversed, while noting that every audience needs its own mix, as a gentle teacher from Homs learned in his rough mountain village. Accountability is the first premise: if consciousness simply ends, there is no conversation, yet the drive to live and an inborn conscience point to purpose. The third bal names the real problem: people love the immediate and neglect the hereafter, like his four-year-old. Loving Allah's world is fine; the danger is holding possessions in the heart, the weakness the Prophet called love of this world and dislike of death, which stops people from ever taking a stand. Radiant faces will look at their Lord, a joy greater than Paradise, while others sense a calamity that strips everything. At death the soul reaches the collarbones, no healer helps, the legs entwine in pain, and the one who neither believed nor prayed is told what would have been better. He urges ranking deeds by priority, citing Jurayj. The surah ends by asking whether man thinks he is left aimless, and whether the One who formed him from a drop cannot raise the dead.

outline.heading: Recap: a cluster on representing Islam
outline.gist: This juz moves from what representation requires to examples of it, ending with three surahs that model dawah.

outline.heading: Three modes of dawah, in sequence
outline.gist: Al-Qiyamah speaks to the intellect and the next two to desire and fear. All are valid motives, but the mind must be engaged first or a person is prepared for catastrophe.

outline.heading: Young Canadians who lost their faith
outline.gist: He has watched many young Muslims here leave Islam, not over anything wrong in it but because it was fed to them in the wrong order; an hour cannot undo fifteen years of poor representation.

outline.heading: Recap: the Day Allah takes a stand on you
outline.gist: We now decide who Allah is to us; on that Day we fall silent and He passes judgment.

outline.heading: Recap: conscience and full insight
outline.gist: Others know only the story you tell, but you know exactly what you did and why, which means you can change.

outline.heading: Recap: the one who hurries through his book
outline.gist: Of the two readings of verses 16-19, he prefers the person on the Day speeding past what he dislikes in his record, whom Allah slows down and clarifies everything for.

outline.heading: The surah calls through judgment itself
outline.gist: Aside from Paradise and Hell, the most important part of the Day is the judgment, and the surah's dawah centres on it.

outline.heading: No one likes to be questioned
outline.gist: Before outcomes, simply being held to account should make us brake: think of court proceedings, a police stop or being made to stand in class.

outline.heading: Accept accountability or the conversation ends
outline.gist: If you believe consciousness disappears into nothing, there is no point continuing; the surah opened by saying it will all come back.

outline.heading: A psyche only possible with purpose
outline.gist: A meaningless life would not want to survive, yet living things cling to life. Where does that come from?

outline.heading: Why would the first cell want to live?
outline.gist: Even granting that life arose spontaneously in a volcanic pool, nothing explains the programming that makes it want to live.

outline.heading: Humans have what animals lack
outline.gist: Lying raises the heart rate and shows on the face. Animals do not contemplate mortality, face moral dilemmas or have existential crises.

outline.heading: The drive to live needs an explanation
outline.gist: The DNA that lets us adapt and every creature's fight for life and space is accepted as a law no one asks about. The surah does not argue; it points out what you already know.

outline.heading: Conditioning erases conscience, not builds it
outline.gist: Nineteenth-century claims that conscience is a social construct failed: remote peoples have it, and brutal killers had to be conditioned to lose it.

outline.heading: You know you are not alone
outline.gist: Deep down you know your life is more than this; giving up the wish for blame-free freedom brings growth, ethics and peace of mind, though it takes sacrifice.

outline.heading: Every dawah touches all three
outline.gist: None of the three surahs uses one approach alone; each emphasizes one according to its audience.

outline.heading: A gentle teacher among mountain people
outline.gist: In his rough rural village a tender-hearted sheikh from Homs, of the Prophet's descendants, preached love with little effect. The young Adnan urged him to speak of fear instead; after one such khutbah the next Fajr was so full the teacher thought there was a funeral.

outline.heading: Different locks need different keys
outline.gist: The one representing Islam must find what moves a given people. Diverse audiences make this hard; homogeneous groups make it easier.

outline.heading: Recitation from verse twenty
outline.gist: He recites the passage, asking listeners to note two different letters.

outline.heading: Dad and dha are different letters
outline.gist: In one the tongue stays inside, in the other it comes out. Some regions merge them, but in the Quran they sound and mean different things.

outline.heading: The third bal
outline.gist: First the bones, then wanting guilt-free freedom, then insight people refuse to admit, as comfortable lies that everyone may believe except Allah. Nowhere else does the Quran stack bal like this.

outline.heading: You love the immediate, like a four-year-old
outline.gist: He and his four-year-old both want what they want now; he has only learned to mask it. Humans choose short gratification over lasting delayed reward.

outline.heading: Nothing wrong with loving the world
outline.gist: This world is Allah's creation, where the Quran was revealed and the Prophet lived; it is beautiful and worth loving.

outline.heading: Despise the low life, not life
outline.gist: What scholars condemn is surrendering to instinct, greed, food, sex, status and power. Good deeds, bravery and sacrifice only happen here.

outline.heading: Hold possessions in the hand, not the heart
outline.gist: Do not invest your heart and ego in your car or house. Many Muslims misread the teaching and come to hate life itself.

outline.heading: Creation is how we come to know Allah
outline.gist: We learn His names and stand in awe of Him through what He created. The problem is a love of the world that makes us flee death.

outline.heading: Wahn: love of the world and dislike of death
outline.gist: Nations will devour Muslims despite their numbers because of wahn, the Prophet explained: clinging to possessions and hating death.

outline.heading: Living any life rather than die
outline.gist: Disliking death is natural; letting it guide every decision produces lives without principle or dignity and people who never speak the truth when it is risky.

outline.heading: Belief worth dying for
outline.gist: A belief you would not give your life for is only a convenience. The world is meant to serve you, not you it.

outline.heading: Seeing the Day through the faces
outline.gist: The Quran often turns your head from the cosmic events to the faces of those witnessing them.

outline.heading: Radiant faces looking at their Lord
outline.gist: Nadirah means relaxed and well watered, rare in the Arabian desert; on a long, thirsty day these faces are fresh as they gaze at their Lord.

outline.heading: Something better than Paradise
outline.gist: In Muslim's narration Allah asks the people of Paradise if they want more, then lifts the veil, and they see Him as clearly as the full moon.

outline.heading: Faces dark and shriveled
outline.gist: No joy in Paradise means more than seeing Him. Other faces are dark and shriveled, sensing what is coming.

outline.heading: Faqirah: a calamity that strips everything
outline.gist: From the root of poverty: an event that takes away all they love and find meaningful.

outline.heading: The small seen on man raq
outline.gist: Hafs's recitation marks a brief pause without breath after the nun; other readings merge it into the ra, and a reciter doing so is not wrong.

outline.heading: Pausing so meaning is not lost
outline.gist: Merged, the phrase can sound like a word for a soup maker; the Prophet recited in ways that kept listeners from misunderstanding, and the Quran has a few such pauses.

outline.heading: The soul reaches the collarbones
outline.gist: Taraqi are the clavicles: the spirit leaves the body from the feet upward until only its exit remains.

outline.heading: Who can heal him?
outline.gist: Raqi comes from ruqyah; in ancient Arabia the healer was also sorcerer, dentist and butcher. Those around the dying ask if anyone can save him.

outline.heading: He knows it is the parting
outline.gist: The dying person is certain it is time to say farewell.

outline.heading: Shin wound around shin: two readings
outline.gist: Either a divine act we accept as stated, or an Arab idiom, common in their poetry, for the arrival of hardship and catastrophe.

outline.heading: Pain even the righteous feel
outline.gist: People cross their legs in pain, as a child does at a flu shot. Even those who love meeting Allah feel death's agonies, as the Prophet said.

outline.heading: Born crying, leaving in pain
outline.gist: We enter life and leave it with discomfort. To your Lord that Day is the driving: you are taken in a direction you did not choose.

outline.heading: He neither believed nor prayed
outline.gist: The departing soul had no true belief or connection with Allah shown in its behaviour.

outline.heading: Denied, turned away, strutted home
outline.gist: Takdhib is intellectual rejection of what he knew was true, tawalli is physically turning from prayer, and he went home full of himself.

outline.heading: Awla laka: what would have been better
outline.gist: Many scholars read it as a threat of woe, but he takes it linguistically: this was more fitting for you, a matter of priority.

outline.heading: Choose what is best, then the next best
outline.gist: While still alive, rank your choices and start with what matters most, because at death there are no extensions.

outline.heading: Not only good deeds but the right order
outline.gist: Praying sunnah while a family member in need goes without your help or wealth counts for nothing.

outline.heading: Jurayj and his mother's call
outline.gist: Jurayj kept praying voluntary prayer while his mother called, and her dua against him nearly ruined him; answering her mattered more.

outline.heading: It comes sooner than you hope
outline.gist: Death always comes too soon, unless one reaches the worst stage of life, unaware and a burden to others.

outline.heading: Regret at the collarbones
outline.gist: At that moment your life races through your mind: choices, sins and postponed deeds you can no longer fix. He recites the final verses.

outline.heading: The raw human being, unmasked
outline.gist: No surah of its length repeats insan so often; it strips away every description to address the human as he is.

outline.heading: Suda: going nowhere
outline.gist: Does man think he will be left aimless, with no destination, so any direction is as good as another and nothing is accountable?

outline.heading: Wild camels and livestock
outline.gist: Suda described wild camels that simply exist, unlike herds kept for milk, meat and hides. Man let himself believe he was like them.

outline.heading: How he arrived at aimlessness
outline.gist: The surah's chain: doubt about resurrection, wanting guilt-free sin, ignoring his own insight, and loving immediate gratification.

outline.heading: Once a drop, then a clot
outline.gist: Was he not a drop of fluid, then a clot so small you would flick it off your hand?

outline.heading: Formed, balanced and made in pairs
outline.gist: Allah proportioned him with ears, eyes and mind and made male and female to build families, progeny and meaning.

outline.heading: Is not that One able to raise the dead?
outline.gist: Dhalika points to the whole process of creation; the surah ends with a question, returning to its opening doubt about gathering the bones.

outline.heading: You will never exist again
outline.gist: Your DNA sequence is one of almost infinite possibilities and will never repeat; you are one of a kind, yet you drifted into thinking yourself aimless.

outline.heading: You must answer the question
outline.gist: If the answer is yes, your choices must reflect it; if no, you have chosen how to live.

32:3.ar: أَمۡ يَقُولُونَ ٱفۡتَرَىٰهُۚ بَلۡ هُوَ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ لِتُنذِرَ قَوۡمࣰ ا مَّآ أَتَىٰهُم مِّن نَّذِيرࣲ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَهۡتَدُونَ
32:3.en: Or say they: He hath invented it? Nay, but it is the Truth from thy Lord, that thou mayst warn a folk to whom no warner came before thee, that haply they may walk aright

32:4.ar: ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ وَمَا بَيۡنَهُمَا فِي سِتَّةِ أَيَّامࣲ ثُمَّ ٱسۡتَوَىٰ عَلَى ٱلۡعَرۡشِۖ مَا لَكُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَلِيࣲّ وَلَا شَفِيعٍۚ أَفَلَا تَتَذَكَّرُونَ
32:4.en: Allah it is Who created the heavens and the earth, and that which is between them, in six Days. Then He mounted the Throne. Ye have not, beside Him, a protecting friend or mediator. Will ye not then remember

32:5.ar: يُدَبِّرُ ٱلۡأَمۡرَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِلَى ٱلۡأَرۡضِ ثُمَّ يَعۡرُجُ إِلَيۡهِ فِي يَوۡمࣲ كَانَ مِقۡدَارُهُۥٓ أَلۡفَ سَنَةࣲ مِّمَّا تَعُدُّونَ
32:5.en: He directeth the ordinance from the heaven unto the earth; then it ascendeth unto Him in a Day, whereof the measure is a thousand years of that ye reckon

32:6.ar: ذَٰلِكَ عَٰلِمُ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
32:6.en: Such is the Knower of the Invisible and the Visible, the Mighty, the Merciful

32:7.ar: ٱلَّذِيٓ أَحۡسَنَ كُلَّ شَيۡءٍ خَلَقَهُۥۖ وَبَدَأَ خَلۡقَ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنِ مِن طِينࣲ‏
32:7.en: Who made all things good which He created, and He began the creation of man from clay

32:8.ar: ثُمَّ جَعَلَ نَسۡلَهُۥ مِن سُلَٰلَةࣲ مِّن مَّآءࣲ مَّهِينࣲ‏
32:8.en: Then He made his seed from a draught of despised fluid

32:9.ar: ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰهُ وَنَفَخَ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِهِۦۖ وَجَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلسَّمۡعَ وَٱلۡأَبۡصَٰرَ وَٱلۡأَفۡـِٔدَةَۚ قَلِيلࣰ ا مَّا تَشۡكُرُونَ
32:9.en: Then He fashioned him and breathed into him of His Spirit; and appointed for you hearing and sight and hearts. Small thanks give ye

32:10.ar: وَقَالُوٓاْ أَءِذَا ضَلَلۡنَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ أَءِنَّا لَفِي خَلۡقࣲ جَدِيدِۭۚ بَلۡ هُم بِلِقَآءِ رَبِّهِمۡ كَٰفِرُونَ
32:10.en: And they say: When we are lost in the earth, how can we then be re-created? Nay but they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord

32:11.ar: ۞قُلۡ يَتَوَفَّىٰكُم مَّلَكُ ٱلۡمَوۡتِ ٱلَّذِي وُكِّلَ بِكُمۡ ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمۡ تُرۡجَعُونَ
32:11.en: Say: The angel of death, who hath charge concerning you, will gather you, and afterward unto your Lord ye will be returned

32:12.ar: وَلَوۡ تَرَىٰٓ إِذِ ٱلۡمُجۡرِمُونَ نَاكِسُواْ رُءُوسِهِمۡ عِندَ رَبِّهِمۡ رَبَّنَآ أَبۡصَرۡنَا وَسَمِعۡنَا فَٱرۡجِعۡنَا نَعۡمَلۡ صَٰلِحًا إِنَّا مُوقِنُونَ
32:12.en: Couldst thou but see when the guilty hang their heads before their Lord, (and say): Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back; we will do right, now we are sure

21:23.ar: لَا يُسۡـَٔلُ عَمَّا يَفۡعَلُ وَهُمۡ يُسۡـَٔلُونَ
21:23.en: He will not be questioned as to that which He doeth, but they will be questioned

6:99.ar: وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أَنزَلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءࣰ فَأَخۡرَجۡنَا بِهِۦ نَبَاتَ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ فَأَخۡرَجۡنَا مِنۡهُ خَضِرࣰ ا نُّخۡرِجُ مِنۡهُ حَبࣰّ ا مُّتَرَاكِبࣰ ا وَمِنَ ٱلنَّخۡلِ مِن طَلۡعِهَا قِنۡوَانࣱ دَانِيَةࣱ وَجَنَّٰتࣲ مِّنۡ أَعۡنَابࣲ وَٱلزَّيۡتُونَ وَٱلرُّمَّانَ مُشۡتَبِهࣰ ا وَغَيۡرَ مُتَشَٰبِهٍۗ ٱنظُرُوٓاْ إِلَىٰ ثَمَرِهِۦٓ إِذَآ أَثۡمَرَ وَيَنۡعِهِۦٓۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكُمۡ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّقَوۡمࣲ يُؤۡمِنُونَ
6:99.en: He it is Who sendeth down water from the sky, and therewith We bring forth buds of every kind; We bring forth the green blade from which We bring forth the thick-clustered grain; and from the date-palm, from the pollen thereof, spring pendant bunches; and (We bring forth) gardens of grapes, and the olive and the pomegranate, alike and unlike. Look upon the fruit thereof, when they bear fruit, and upon its ripening. Lo! herein verily are portents for a people who believe

29:20.ar: قُلۡ سِيرُواْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ فَٱنظُرُواْ كَيۡفَ بَدَأَ ٱلۡخَلۡقَۚ ثُمَّ ٱللَّهُ يُنشِئُ ٱلنَّشۡأَةَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرࣱ‏
29:20.en: Say (O Muhammad): Travel in the land and see how He originated creation, then Allah bringeth forth the later growth. Lo! Allah is Able to do all things

17:23.ar: ۞وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعۡبُدُوٓاْ إِلَّآ إِيَّاهُ وَبِٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ إِحۡسَٰنًاۚ إِمَّا يَبۡلُغَنَّ عِندَكَ ٱلۡكِبَرَ أَحَدُهُمَآ أَوۡ كِلَاهُمَا فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَآ أُفࣲّ وَلَا تَنۡهَرۡهُمَا وَقُل لَّهُمَا قَوۡلࣰ ا كَرِيمࣰ ا
17:23.en: Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents. If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word

17:85.ar: وَيَسۡـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلرُّوحِۖ قُلِ ٱلرُّوحُ مِنۡ أَمۡرِ رَبِّي وَمَآ أُوتِيتُم مِّنَ ٱلۡعِلۡمِ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا
17:85.en: They are asking thee concerning the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is by command of my Lord, and of knowledge ye have been vouchsafed but little

4:78.ar: أَيۡنَمَا تَكُونُواْ يُدۡرِككُّمُ ٱلۡمَوۡتُ وَلَوۡ كُنتُمۡ فِي بُرُوجࣲ مُّشَيَّدَةࣲۗ وَإِن تُصِبۡهُمۡ حَسَنَةࣱ يَقُولُواْ هَٰذِهِۦ مِنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِۖ وَإِن تُصِبۡهُمۡ سَيِّئَةࣱ يَقُولُواْ هَٰذِهِۦ مِنۡ عِندِكَۚ قُلۡ كُلࣱّ مِّنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِۖ فَمَالِ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ لَا يَكَادُونَ يَفۡقَهُونَ حَدِيثࣰ ا
4:78.en: Wheresoever ye may be, death will overtake you, even though ye were in lofty towers. Yet if a happy thing befalleth them they say: This is from Allah; and if an evil thing befalleth them they say: This is of thy doing (O Muhammad). Say (unto them): All is from Allah. What is amiss with these people that they come not nigh to understand a happening

19:57.en: And We raised him to high station

qHSRsGx35Mk.speaker: adnan
qHSRsGx35Mk.speaker_note: his weekly Arabic tafsir; continues his As-Sajdah series from the previous week in his own voice
qHSRsGx35Mk.title: Arabic Tafseer: Surah As-Sajdah (32:1-12)
qHSRsGx35Mk.one_line: As-Sajdah as the surah of our relationship with Allah: creation from clay as the ground of gratitude, then death, the meeting with Allah and regret.
qHSRsGx35Mk.summary: Continuing As-Sajdah, which he calls the surah of the most important relationship, the one with Allah, he notes that the Prophet recited it at Fajr on Friday to open each week with that reminder. Allah began the conversation by sending His book, so our dua is a reply. He needs nothing from creation, there is no intermediary between us and Him, and the names Knower of the unseen, Almighty and Merciful are the minimum anyone must know of Him. Most of the lesson explains why verses 7 to 9 put progeny before fashioning and the breathing of the spirit: he reads them as humanity born gradually from the womb of the earth rather than from a mother's womb, argues that Islam has no quarrel with the natural development of life, cites early Muslim thinkers such as al-Jahiz, and insists science explains how while the Quran explains who and why. The gift of hearing, sight and an aware heart, prepared over billions of years, is the root blessing people take for granted while treating Allah like a relative who only calls to ask for money. Moving to verses 10 to 12, he stresses that resurrection is a meeting with one's Lord, that the angel of death is assigned to each of us, and that the criminals' plea to be sent back comes too late.

outline.heading: The surah of the most important relationship
outline.gist: As-Sajdah closes a group of surahs on relationships with the one that matters most; whoever sets it right finds everything else in life set right.

outline.heading: Recited at Fajr on Friday; Allah spoke to you first
outline.gist: The Prophet opened each week with it; the Quran is Allah's address to you, so your dua is a reply in an ongoing conversation.

outline.heading: Created in six days, then rose over the throne: He needs nothing
outline.gist: Creation was not for any need of His; and there is no protector or intercessor besides Him, so speak to Him directly.

outline.heading: A day of a thousand years by His reckoning
outline.gist: He directs affairs from heaven to earth and people's responses rise back to Him; His days are not our twenty-four hours.

outline.heading: Three names no relationship can do without
outline.gist: Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Almighty who is not questioned, and the Merciful whose mercy is directed at you.

outline.heading: Why progeny comes before fashioning and the spirit
outline.gist: The use of thumma implies sequence, so clay, then generations from a lowly fluid, then fashioning and breath cannot describe a single birth.

outline.heading: Humanity born from the womb of the earth
outline.gist: The verses describe life emerging gradually from the earth; Islam has no problem with the natural development of creatures, and the claim that man came from a monkey misreads the idea.

outline.heading: Extinctions, and all of creation leading to you
outline.gist: Life was wiped out several times and rose again; the aim of it all was to reach the human being. He is not defending a theory but refusing to make religion an enemy of science.

outline.heading: Do not fight science with religion
outline.gist: Theories are answered by theories; Catholic leaders once lost both worlds this way, while early Muslims like Ikhwan al-Safa and al-Jahiz wrote about the development of creatures.

outline.heading: Science gives the how, the Quran the who and why
outline.gist: The Quran tells us to travel and see how creation began; the more we understand the how, the more we glorify and love the Creator.

outline.heading: Fashioned, then the breath of the spirit: Adam
outline.gist: Once the human reached the right form, Allah breathed His spirit into him, giving awareness, speech, questioning and reasoning, and so Adam became accountable.

outline.heading: Hearing, sight and an aware heart
outline.gist: These are listed after the breath because they are the windows of consciousness, unlike the instinct-serving senses of animals.

outline.heading: Camels for a million years versus two men for ten
outline.gist: Animals stay as they were while humans transform the earth; the gift of the fu'ad is extraordinary, yet little do you thank.

outline.heading: The story of creation told for the sake of the relationship
outline.gist: From the first organism in a volcanic pool to the upright human who looked at the sky and received the spirit, all of it was so you could know and connect with your Creator.

outline.heading: Being alive and aware is the root blessing
outline.gist: People take existence for granted and only count money, looks or status as blessings, forgetting the original gift.

outline.heading: The breath of His spirit: affirm without imagining
outline.gist: We may not picture how Allah breathed His spirit; we affirm the meaning that something from Him was placed in us in a way befitting His majesty.

outline.heading: Fourteen billion years and a life of complaints
outline.gist: It took billions of years to bring you into being, yet people spend their sixty or seventy years complaining as if that cancels it all.

outline.heading: A give-me-only relationship
outline.gist: Like a relative who only calls to ask for money, many treat Allah with nothing but demands while ignoring all He already gave.

outline.heading: Tawhid, then kindness to parents
outline.gist: Wiping the slate clean with Allah is like telling parents at forty that their years of care do not count; whoever does not recognize either favour has understood nothing.

outline.heading: Gratitude is the first point of the relationship
outline.gist: Allah does not tire as some claim; if the heart is not full of gratitude for being created, the relationship cannot last.

outline.heading: Interlude
When we are lost in the earth
outline.gist: The deniers point to bodies decomposing into scattered molecules, from a hundred billion people; yet the One who brought you out once can bring you out again.

outline.heading: Their real problem: denying the meeting with their Lord
outline.gist: Allah chose the word liqa rather than resurrection; you will meet Him, see Him and speak to Him, and you only look forward to meeting someone you know.

outline.heading: The angel of death assigned to you
outline.gist: The soul breathed into you belongs to Allah, and an angel is entrusted with taking it back before you return to your Lord.

outline.heading: The soul is beyond our knowledge
outline.gist: Neuroscience maps neurons but barely understands consciousness; modern medication manages effects rather than understanding the mind.

outline.heading: No escape from death: ask for a good ending
outline.gist: However long life seems, it is short; follow the Prophet in often asking Allah for a good end.

outline.heading: Idris and the angel of death
outline.gist: An Israelite report in Ibn Kathir has Idris carried to the heavens to seek more life, only for the angel of death to say he was ordered to take his soul there.

outline.heading: The relationship exists; you decide its quality
outline.gist: Willing or not, Allah spoke to you and you will meet Him; breathing His spirit into you expresses closeness and His wish that the relationship be good.

outline.heading: Heads hung low: we have seen and heard, send us back
outline.gist: The criminals finally use the hearing, sight and hearts they were given and claim certainty, but the words that would have saved them in this world are useless now.

outline.heading: A lifetime is a blink in the cosmos
outline.gist: Begging for one more brief return shows a broken relationship: they meet Allah and speak to Him, but with words that no longer help.

outline.heading: Outro

EdRLxcTnRZg.speaker: adnan
EdRLxcTnRZg.speaker_note: continues his own Tazkiyah mortality series and refers to his medical work
EdRLxcTnRZg.title: Tazkiyah Halaqa: Mortality, Episode 24
EdRLxcTnRZg.one_line: Mortality can only be accepted as a transition, not nothingness, and we must replace the nafs' comforting lie with the truth.
EdRLxcTnRZg.summary: He asks what humans really fear about death and answers: nothingness, the end of consciousness, which magnifies the fear of being left out. Seen that way, death can never truly be accepted, which is why most people ignore it, while pre-Islamic Arabs swung to the other extreme and obsessed over an honourable death. Islam reframes death as a transition, like birth from the womb into a vast world; the grave is the first stage of the hereafter, and resurrection was one of only two arguments the Prophet had with Quraysh. This changes the fear from non-existence to a healthy fear of not having done enough, which motivates action, as seen in Umar's humility at his death. He then describes an exercise of living as if this is your last week, and explains it fails because it is a lie, yet people readily accept the nafs' opposite lie that they have plenty of time. The truth is that you will probably live for years but the possibility of death is never zero. Using fire safety, medical training and bike helmets, he argues we prepare for rare risks everywhere else. If you would change something on learning you were dying, change it now.

outline.heading: Recap: accepting mortality makes finite time precious
outline.gist: Accepting mortality brings sadness first, then beautifies life because finite time cannot be regenerated.

outline.heading: What we really fear: nothingness
outline.gist: Humans fear the end of consciousness; seen that way, death cannot be accepted, only tolerated.

outline.heading: The fear of being left out
outline.gist: Children and adults suffer deeply from being left out, and death as nothingness magnifies that fear.

outline.heading: Why most people ignore death
outline.gist: Because nothingness is too sad, people keep life a revolving door of activity to avoid thinking about it.

outline.heading: Pre-Islamic Arabs and the obsession with an honourable death
outline.gist: Living close to death, the Arabs embraced it and obsessed over dying honourably, fuelling wars lasting generations.

outline.heading: Two extremes, and the human ability to contemplate death
outline.gist: People swing between celebrating death and ignoring it; unlike animals, humans can contemplate their end.

outline.heading: Be in this world like a stranger or traveller
outline.gist: The Prophet told Ibn Umar to live like a traveller passing through, and Ibn Umar taught not to delay deeds and to use health and life before they go.

outline.heading: Death as transition makes acceptance possible
outline.gist: Mortality can only be accepted when death is seen as moving to another form of life, beginning with barzakh.

outline.heading: The grave as the first stage of the hereafter
outline.gist: Whoever finds the grave easy finds what follows easier; graves are gardens of Paradise or pits of Hell; consciousness continues.

outline.heading: The Prophet's two arguments with Quraysh
outline.gist: He disputed only shirk, which corrupts the relationship with God, and their denial of resurrection.

outline.heading: Fix this belief before anything else
outline.gist: If you still see death as the end, that is the main problem in your deen, and the rest of Islam cannot stand until it is corrected.

outline.heading: From fear of non-existence to a healthy fear
outline.gist: As a transition, death's fear becomes losing the chance to repent and facing accountability, which motivates action rather than flight.

outline.heading: The womb and the world
outline.gist: A baby leaves the womb crying, yet the world is vast compared to it; every transition moves to something bigger.

outline.heading: Why the companions faced death openly
outline.gist: They knew what was coming; what is lost at death is not existence but the chance to improve.

outline.heading: The believer's question: am I ready?
outline.gist: When Allah calls you home, the fear is whether you have something worth showing or will be ashamed.

outline.heading: Too late to realise, and what Muslims gain
outline.gist: Most people waste life fearing nothingness; accepting mortality helps anyone, but does far more for a Muslim.

outline.heading: The exercise: live as if it is your last week
outline.gist: Most never try; those who do find it hard but come back questioning their choices.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah never asks you to lie to yourself
outline.gist: The exercise fails because it is a lie; tazkiyah is only learning the truth.

outline.heading: The nafs' comfortable lie
outline.gist: We reject the unpleasant lie but happily believe the nafs telling us we are young and have years ahead.

outline.heading: What would you change? Ideally nothing
outline.gist: The right way of life would not change on hearing of death except for a few early farewells; wanting to quit everything signals a bigger problem.

outline.heading: The truth: likely years, but never zero risk
outline.gist: Behaviour must reflect that death is possible at any moment; the comforting lie works like morphine numbing the soul.

outline.heading: Shortening long hopes (tul al-amal)
outline.gist: The early generations shortened their hopes; he leaves it to each person to reconcile planning for this life with readiness to die.

outline.heading: You are not a special case
outline.gist: Millions have died at exactly your age; the possibility must ring true and change you.

outline.heading: The radical answers people give
outline.gist: People say they would give away all their money, quit university or insult their boss, which shows a wrong understanding.

outline.heading: Rising probability makes people straighten up
outline.gist: On a shaking plane or after a diagnosis people change; if the risk is never zero, make the change now.

outline.heading: Analogy: fire safety
outline.gist: We demand fire preparedness for unlikely fires, yet a young person's death is more likely than a building burning.

outline.heading: Studying and work are worship
outline.gist: Wanting to stop studying or working on hearing of death means doing them for the wrong reason, as they are among the best deeds.

outline.heading: The scholars' answer: change nothing
outline.gist: Asked what they would change if they knew they were dying, the righteous said needing to change means being on the wrong track; prayer, family and halal work continue regardless.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet and companions were so selfless
outline.gist: They had internalised that life could end any moment and feared not having done enough.

outline.heading: Umar's death
outline.gist: Stabbed while leading prayer in the Prophet's mosque, he still wished he had never been born, out of fear of accountability, a healthy fear.

outline.heading: Living with the constant possibility ends procrastination
outline.gist: Since the possibility is always there, you stop useless behaviour that does not serve your bigger picture.

outline.heading: Analogies: medical training and bike helmets
outline.gist: Medicine trains for the rare catastrophe and children wear helmets for unlikely falls; life should be prepared the same way.

outline.heading: What are you waiting for?
outline.gist: If there is anything you would change, ask why you are waiting.

outline.heading: Tell yourself the truth
outline.gist: Mortality is a transition, and the truth is you will likely live many years but could die at any moment; living that truth improves you.

outline.heading: Outro

16:90.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأۡمُرُ بِٱلۡعَدۡلِ وَٱلۡإِحۡسَٰنِ وَإِيتَآيِٕ ذِي ٱلۡقُرۡبَىٰ وَيَنۡهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلۡفَحۡشَآءِ وَٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَٱلۡبَغۡيِۚ يَعِظُكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَذَكَّرُونَ
16:90.en: Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbiddeth lewdness and abomination and wickedness. He exhorteth you in order that ye may take heed

16:91.ar: وَأَوۡفُواْ بِعَهۡدِ ٱللَّهِ إِذَا عَٰهَدتُّمۡ وَلَا تَنقُضُواْ ٱلۡأَيۡمَٰنَ بَعۡدَ تَوۡكِيدِهَا وَقَدۡ جَعَلۡتُمُ ٱللَّهَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ كَفِيلًاۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا تَفۡعَلُونَ
16:91.en: Fulfil the covenant of Allah when ye have covenanted, and break not your oaths after the asseveration of them, and after ye have made Allah surety over you. Lo! Allah knoweth what ye do

16:92.ar: وَلَا تَكُونُواْ كَٱلَّتِي نَقَضَتۡ غَزۡلَهَا مِنۢ بَعۡدِ قُوَّةٍ أَنكَٰثࣰ ا تَتَّخِذُونَ أَيۡمَٰنَكُمۡ دَخَلَۢا بَيۡنَكُمۡ أَن تَكُونَ أُمَّةٌ هِيَ أَرۡبَىٰ مِنۡ أُمَّةٍۚ إِنَّمَا يَبۡلُوكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦۚ وَلَيُبَيِّنَنَّ لَكُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ مَا كُنتُمۡ فِيهِ تَخۡتَلِفُونَ
16:92.en: And be not like unto her who unravelleth the thread, after she hath made it strong, to thin filaments, making your oaths a deceit between you because of a nation being more numerous than (another) nation. Allah only trieth you thereby, and He verily will explain to you on the Day of Resurrection that wherein ye differed

16:93.ar: وَلَوۡ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَجَعَلَكُمۡ أُمَّةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰ وَلَٰكِن يُضِلُّ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهۡدِي مَن يَشَآءُۚ وَلَتُسۡـَٔلُنَّ عَمَّا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
16:93.en: Had Allah willed He could have made you (all) one nation, but He sendeth whom He will astray and guideth whom He will, and ye will indeed be asked of what ye used to do

16:94.ar: وَلَا تَتَّخِذُوٓاْ أَيۡمَٰنَكُمۡ دَخَلَۢا بَيۡنَكُمۡ فَتَزِلَّ قَدَمُۢ بَعۡدَ ثُبُوتِهَا وَتَذُوقُواْ ٱلسُّوٓءَ بِمَا صَدَدتُّمۡ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَكُمۡ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمࣱ‏
16:94.en: Make not your oaths a deceit between you, lest a foot should slip after being firmly planted and ye should taste evil forasmuch as ye debarred (men) from the way of Allah, and yours should be an awful doom

16:95.ar: وَلَا تَشۡتَرُواْ بِعَهۡدِ ٱللَّهِ ثَمَنࣰ ا قَلِيلًاۚ إِنَّمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
16:95.en: And purchase not a small gain at the price of Allah's covenant. Lo! that which Allah hath is better for you, if ye did but know

16:96.ar: مَا عِندَكُمۡ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقࣲۗ وَلَنَجۡزِيَنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ صَبَرُوٓاْ أَجۡرَهُم بِأَحۡسَنِ مَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
16:96.en: That which ye have wasteth away, and that which Allah hath remaineth. And verily We shall pay those who are steadfast a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do

16:97.ar: مَنۡ عَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ ا مِّن ذَكَرٍ أَوۡ أُنثَىٰ وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنࣱ فَلَنُحۡيِيَنَّهُۥ حَيَوٰةࣰ طَيِّبَةࣰۖ وَلَنَجۡزِيَنَّهُمۡ أَجۡرَهُم بِأَحۡسَنِ مَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
16:97.en: Whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily we shall quicken with good life, and We shall pay them a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do

29:2.ar: أَحَسِبَ ٱلنَّاسُ أَن يُتۡرَكُوٓاْ أَن يَقُولُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا وَهُمۡ لَا يُفۡتَنُونَ
29:2.en: Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction

29:3.ar: وَلَقَدۡ فَتَنَّا ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِهِمۡۖ فَلَيَعۡلَمَنَّ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ صَدَقُواْ وَلَيَعۡلَمَنَّ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ
29:3.en: Lo! We tested those who were before you. Thus Allah knoweth those who are sincere, and knoweth those who feign
