cdxrMr7YQzk.title: Listening to the Divine: An-Nahl 90-97, Part 2
cdxrMr7YQzk.one_line: Finishing An-Nahl 90-97: the verse that settled Uthman ibn Maz'un's faith, the covenant that is not for sale, promised trials, and the good life.
cdxrMr7YQzk.summary: Part two of his khutbah on An-Nahl 90-97, finishing the commentary he could not complete the week before. He first shows the weight of 16:90, the verse every khutbah closes with: Imam Ahmad records that Uthman ibn Maz'un, a wealthy Qurayshi who had accepted Islam only out of shyness before the Prophet, said faith settled in his heart when he heard it, and when the Prophet offered himself to twenty-six tribes in ten days, Mafruq of Banu Shayban recognized in it a call to noble character. The verses then turn to the covenant: do not make or unravel commitments out of self-interest, fear or siding with the stronger party, because everything you have runs out; a man who sold his principles enjoys the gain for forty years and regrets it in his seventies with the grave in view. Everyone has a price, so is your covenant with Allah for sale? Even supreme leadership of the planet would leave you cheap. The Quran promises the individual nothing in this world except trials and does not soften that to market itself. Its single worldly promise is the good life of 16:97, which the Arabic second khutbah locates not in wealth, status or health but in a tranquil heart with a purpose beyond its instincts.

outline.heading: Opening
He commands and He forbids
outline.gist: Allah opens by stating that He commands certain things and prohibits others; that emphasis is why these verses are always recited in khutbahs, and accepting them is entering a covenant.

outline.heading: Uthman ibn Maz'un: the verse that settled his faith
outline.gist: Imam Ahmad's narration: a wealthy Qurayshi who admired the Prophet's selflessness accepted Islam out of shyness, unsure of it, until these verses were recited and faith settled in his heart.

outline.heading: Twenty-six tribes in ten days
outline.gist: In the tenth year of prophethood the Prophet presented himself to tribe after tribe, exhausting days of refusals and insults, until Banu Shayban gave a reasonable hearing and their leader Mafruq ibn Amr asked what he was calling to.

outline.heading: Mafruq: you call to noble character
outline.gist: On hearing 16:90 Mafruq said he was calling to noble character and good deeds and that those who denied him had wronged themselves, though his tribe could not offer protection.

outline.heading: Listen to Allah directly
outline.gist: Spend less time listening to people like him; Allah is addressing you as an individual. The imam's only function is to help you understand the Book, and imams carry no other status.

outline.heading: Covenants made from interest or fear
outline.gist: After the commands and prohibitions comes the covenant: do not be like the woman who unravelled her yarn, and do not make or break covenants for personal benefit, to be on the stronger side, or out of fear or greed.

outline.heading: All you have is finite
outline.gist: Do not use oaths as a means of corruption, because everything in this world runs out: you enjoy the gain in your thirties, forties and fifties, then sickness comes and nothing matters.

outline.heading: Regret at seventy
outline.gist: Old and tired, with the grave beyond the horizon, you regret forty years of standing by what you knew was wrong because a tribe, country or way of life was popular or profitable, and you can no longer enjoy what you gained.

outline.heading: Is your covenant for sale?
outline.gist: Hold to justice, excellence and the rest to the end. Someday someone will put a price on your word and loyalty; everyone is for sale at the right price. Even supreme leadership of the earth would make you cheap and the covenant cheaply sold.

outline.heading: Selling out subtly: selective justice
outline.gist: Selling the covenant can mean being fair only to people you like and not to a group that looks, smells or speaks differently; and whatever you gain runs out.

outline.heading: Promised nothing but trials
outline.gist: The individual is promised nothing in this world. Did people think they would say 'we believe' and not be tested? Allah tests to make known who was truthful and who lied.

outline.heading: Trials are part of the covenant
outline.gist: Trials are promised, not a possibility: whoever believes should prepare for tribulation, and the most tested are the prophets, then the righteous, then the next best.

outline.heading: Allah does not need to market His teachings
outline.gist: From a marketing standpoint promising trials is a poor pitch, but there is no lying in this story; Allah does not soften the consequences. Accept the covenant and stand by it.

outline.heading: Hayat tayyibah: the ripe fruit
outline.gist: Whoever does good as a believer, male or female, receives a good life. Tayyib describes ripe fruit, full of water and sweetness, where unripe fruit is empty and sour.

outline.heading: A life with purpose beyond instinct
outline.gist: The good life is fulfilment: a life that meant something beyond basic needs and urges, aimed at a goal Allah beautified, that you look back on at peace and can sleep on each night, rich or poor, healthy or sick, long or short.

outline.heading: The more you get, the more you need
outline.gist: Every human seeks fulfilment whether they know it or not; the young do not see it yet, but later they eat, travel and gather a great deal and are never filled by it.

outline.heading: Interlude
The one worldly promise to the individual
outline.gist: Every Quranic promise to believers concerns the Hereafter; the ummah is promised establishment on earth, but the individual only repeated trials and the command to be patient, except for this verse. It does not promise long life, health or power.

outline.heading: The good life lives in the heart
outline.gist: We ask Allah for wealth, health and status but are not promised them; the intelligent person knows quality of life lies in a tranquil heart filled with closeness to its Lord that knows its purpose.

outline.heading: Sheikh, I am tired
outline.gist: Living for something higher than oneself is what humans have sought since creation; the man whose wealth, travel, food, friends and children multiply yet feels empty is seeking tranquility in the wrong place. Fulfil the covenant: justice, excellence, giving to kin.

outline.heading: Outro

09hZDtvueqM.title: Tazkiyah Halaqa: Mortality, Episode 25
09hZDtvueqM.one_line: Immortality would be a curse; mortality reveals what matters, and facing death needs balanced fear and hope grounded in truly knowing Allah.
09hZDtvueqM.summary: He begins by insisting death is always sad and that the aim is to stop running from it, not to stop grieving. He recounts a philosophical debate on whether to drink an immortality potion and sides with the view that endless life would be a curse: everything turns boring and you lose any stable sense of self and values, while standing at a deathbed makes clear what matters. Paradise is designed differently, and death being slaughtered at the end only means something to those who knew mortality. Returning to his 'last week to live' exercise, he challenges answers like quitting work or study, which reveal a weak grasp of the deen or of intention. He then turns to the fear of accountability, which must be balanced by hope, and that balance depends on knowing Allah as the Quran and Prophet describe Him rather than a self-made god. You can never be ready by deeds, only by walking the path with humility, love and repentance. He illustrates with the camel's mercy, companions who wept and smiled at death, a young cousin dying of leukemia in his village, and the man who claimed Paradise by his deeds. The truthful position: you will likely live long and hope for Paradise, but neither is guaranteed.

outline.heading: Death stays sad, but stop running from it
outline.gist: As a physician he has seen many deaths and it never gets easier; the goal is to embrace death as inevitable, not to stop feeling sad.

outline.heading: The immortality potion: endless life becomes boring
outline.gist: Philosophers have long debated whether to drink a potion granting immortality; the most compelling answer is that everything would become unbearably repetitive.

outline.heading: Without an end you lose your sense of self
outline.gist: Constantly reinventing yourself forever would destroy any stable identity, and without an end you cannot discover your values or priorities.

outline.heading: A deathbed shows what matters
outline.gist: Witnessing a death makes it easy to see what is important and what never deserved a moment of worry.

outline.heading: Paradise is built differently from this world
outline.gist: Immortality here would be a curse; people in Paradise are happily occupied, while this world was designed to end so we learn the value of time.

outline.heading: Death slaughtered between Paradise and Hell
outline.gist: At the end, death is brought in the form of a ram and slaughtered, and only those who experienced mortality can appreciate never dying again.

outline.heading: Keep death in the background, not in control
outline.gist: No one should live gripped by death, but it must stay part of the equation; the truth lies between 'I die tomorrow' and 'I have plenty of time'.

outline.heading: The Prophet's lines in the sand
outline.gist: He drew a person's long hope, his lifespan and the misfortunes that cut him off; death never comes at the right time.

outline.heading: The exercise: what overarching themes would you change?
outline.gist: Set aside farewells and extra prayer; ask whether the big themes of your life would change if you had a week.

outline.heading: Quitting your job shows a weak grasp of the deen
outline.gist: Sitting home reading Quran is never better than earning halal income and caring for dependants; if work feels meaningless, ask why.

outline.heading: Stopping study, and the role of intention
outline.gist: No act of worship beats seeking knowledge; usually the action is fine and it is the understanding and intention that need fixing.

outline.heading: Habits you really should drop
outline.gist: Some changes are right, such as quitting smoking or binge-watching; the exercise is meant to test why you do what you do.

outline.heading: When life feels meaningless
outline.gist: Radical change with a good intention is healthy; it is sad when people stay in meaningless lives out of fear, and nearness to death pushes reassessment.

outline.heading: The fear of accountability needs balance
outline.gist: A Muslim's fear is facing his record before Allah, not nothingness, but an unbalanced fear backfires.

outline.heading: The wise one and the fool
outline.gist: The wise person holds himself accountable and works for after death; the fool follows his desires and engages in wishful thinking about Allah.

outline.heading: Fear joined to hope through knowing Allah
outline.gist: How you view death depends on how you understand Allah: fearful of your shortcomings, hopeful in His mercy and love.

outline.heading: Whoever loves to meet Allah
outline.gist: Allah loves to meet those who love to meet Him; when asked about disliking death, the Prophet clarified he did not mean natural dislike of death.

outline.heading: 'I am as My servant thinks of Me'
outline.gist: Your assumption about Allah must be an educated one built on proper understanding, not wishful thinking.

outline.heading: Worshipping a self-made god
outline.gist: Many worship a version of Allah tailored to their choices, who cares about their good deeds and ignores their bad ones.

outline.heading: Prophets were sent so people know Allah
outline.gist: Faiths differ in how they understand God; prophets recite His signs so people know Him, and death is described again and again as returning to Him.

outline.heading: 'God is not calling you home yet'
outline.gist: A senior physician he worked with framed death to cancer patients as being called home, which matches the Islamic view.

outline.heading: You are never prepared by deeds
outline.gist: Thinking your deeds are enough means you have already lost; readiness is not a quantity of deeds.

outline.heading: Readiness as walking the path
outline.gist: Be found walking towards Allah despite failures; a scholar said he would rather be judged by Allah than by his own parents.

outline.heading: The mother camel and Allah's mercy
outline.gist: Watching a camel tenderly position herself to feed her young, the Prophet said Allah is more merciful to His servants than that.

outline.heading: Swinging between fear and hope
outline.gist: The believer moves back and forth between regret over his deeds and trust in Allah's mercy, like waiting for exam results.

outline.heading: Overconfident students fail
outline.gist: Those who walk out of an exam sure of themselves usually fail, while the anxious ones do well; healthy hope admits you could have failed.

outline.heading: Companions weeping and smiling at death
outline.gist: Salman wept that he took more than a traveller's provision despite leaving almost nothing, while a dying companion smiled at meeting the Prophet and his beloved ones.

outline.heading: Never get stuck on one side
outline.gist: Neither despairing of punishment nor assuming all will be fine regardless of conduct is truthful.

outline.heading: The truth about where you are going
outline.gist: You hope Allah forgives you and admits you to Paradise, but the possibility of not making it is real; you must qualify for hope, not earn it.

outline.heading: Living between His names
outline.gist: Knowing Allah as the Most Merciful gives hope, while knowing His other names keeps you accountable; this is how you see death.

outline.heading: His cousin's death from leukemia
outline.gist: At 16 he recited Quran at the deathbed of a gifted young man in his village who prayed Fajr when the mosques were empty; it showed how short and sudden life is.

outline.heading: You are not owed a warning
outline.gist: Notice before death to repent and mend ties is a fortune few receive; assuming you will get it is another self-deception.

outline.heading: Build the heart's state before you meet Him
outline.gist: Humility, gratitude, love, reverence and repentance take time to build; arriving with the wrong attitude goes badly regardless of deeds.

outline.heading: The man who claimed Paradise by his deeds
outline.gist: When he boasted, his eyesight alone outweighed his deeds; the Prophet said even he would enter only if Allah covered him in mercy.

outline.heading: Certainty of death, uncertainty of its time
outline.gist: This keeps you ready to meet the Most Generous with love and humility; then fear of death no longer controls your decisions, though death stays sad.

outline.heading: Outro
Reflection for the week
outline.gist: Think about what you would change if your next meeting with him were your last hour.

32:8.ar: ثُمَّ جَعَلَ نَسۡلَهُۥ مِن سُلَٰلَةࣲ مِّن مَّآءࣲ مَّهِينࣲ‏

2TpzEBFYHeg.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat As-Sajdah (verses 4-9)
2TpzEBFYHeg.one_line: Allah introduces Himself before asking anything: Creator, independent on the Throne, sole protector and intercessor, Knower, Mighty and Merciful, then reminds us to be grateful.
2TpzEBFYHeg.summary: He begins with the night the Syrian regime fell, when he found no one to turn to but Allah and went to the masjid. The lesson: in joy or calamity the first reflex should be returning to Allah, in prostration of gratitude or patience, before celebrating with people. Empty masjids mean empty hearts, and a revival of the ummah will only come when hearts are attached to Allah. He then explains verses 4-9. Allah speaks about Himself first: He created the heavens and earth in six of His days, which are spans of time, not ours. Rising over the Throne signals that He needs nothing; He did not create us for any need, which makes this relationship unique. There is no protector or intercessor besides Him, so the culture of connections and middlemen that people love in worldly life has no place with Allah, not even through the Prophet. He distinguishes what Allah decrees from what humans choose, the deeds that rise back to Him. The names Knower of the unseen and seen, Mighty and Merciful lay the foundations of the bond. He perfected all creation and made opposites so we can recognise beauty. Having given us hearing, sight and understanding, the painful verdict is that we are little grateful.

outline.heading: The night the Syrian regime fell
outline.gist: Overwhelmed by sudden relief after years of oppression, he realised the only one to turn to was Allah and went to sit in the masjid.

outline.heading: The first reflex in joy or calamity: return to Allah
outline.gist: Before celebrating or complaining to people, prostrate in gratitude or in patience, praise Him and seek forgiveness, then thank those who were a means.

outline.heading: Empty masjids, empty hearts
outline.gist: People once brought every piece of news to the masjid; when the houses of Allah emptied, hearts emptied. The next day the masjid filled spontaneously with people praising Allah.

outline.heading: Visiting Allah in His house
outline.gist: As a relationship with parents means visiting them, a relationship with Allah means coming to His house; the believer's heart is attached to the masjid.

outline.heading: Share your joy with Allah before your friends
outline.gist: When good news comes, go to Allah first, then go out, feed people and fulfil your vows.

outline.heading: Darkness before dawn: revival needs hearts attached to Allah
outline.gist: He prays for oppressed Muslim lands and argues an enslaved, ignorant nation cannot rise; the change comes when young and old attach their hearts to Allah.

outline.heading: Why Friday Fajr: the Muslim week starts with Jumuah
outline.gist: The week begins on Friday, and opening it with this surah ties the heart to Allah for the whole week.

outline.heading: Recap: revelation, certainty and guidance
outline.gist: The relationship starts with His speech; He spoke to us before we spoke to Him, without doubt, so that we may be guided.

outline.heading: He speaks of Himself first: Creator of heavens and earth
outline.gist: Before describing what He wants from us, Allah tells us who He is; 'sky' covers everything that is not the earth we stand on.

outline.heading: Six days: His days, not ours
outline.gist: A day is a span of time set by the speaker; scholars read the six as long eras or as night, day and the four seasons. He needs no time, but creation needed time to mature, like the earth cooling.

outline.heading: We are a tiny part of His creation
outline.gist: The verse places us as a small piece within an immense cosmos.

outline.heading: Rising over the Throne: affirming without likening
outline.gist: One may leave its meaning to Allah or interpret it as dominion; Ahl al-Sunnah differ on this, and every position seeks to declare Him free of resemblance to creation.

outline.heading: He created us without needing us
outline.gist: Unlike an employer who hires because he needs workers, Allah gains nothing from us; even our worship benefits only us, making this relationship unlike any other.

outline.heading: Loyalty to the One who made you from nothing
outline.gist: A person is less than a dot in a fourteen-billion-year cosmos; if he cannot love and thank the One who brought him into being, what good is in him?

outline.heading: No protector or intercessor besides Him
outline.gist: Everything returns to Allah, so do not look for anyone else; even the Prophet is your teacher, not a channel you speak to Allah through.

outline.heading: Will you not remember? People keep making idols
outline.gist: After every messenger people forget and fashion idols of stone or of human authorities again.

outline.heading: The culture of connections has no place with Allah
outline.gist: People love skipping the queue through someone they know; whatever one thinks of it in worldly life, anyone claiming to broker your affairs with Allah is a liar.

outline.heading: He directs the affair; a day of a thousand years
outline.gist: Creation and command belong to Him; the Quran's 'day' can be a thousand or fifty thousand years, which the Arabs understood.

outline.heading: His decree versus human choice
outline.gist: What He directs is His decree beyond our control, such as illness and death; the wars and greed of humans are their own choices. Our deeds in response to His decree are what rise to Him.

outline.heading: Recitation of the next passage
outline.gist: He reads the verses on the Knower of the unseen and the creation of man.

outline.heading: Knower of the unseen and the seen
outline.gist: Nothing escapes Him, seen or hidden, so you need not fear that any detail is lost.

outline.heading: Al-Aziz: beyond our questioning
outline.gist: We lack the tools to grasp why He creates, as a four-year-old cannot understand marriage; asking Him to justify Himself is futile.

outline.heading: Ar-Rahim, and the three names as foundations
outline.gist: Though Mighty, He is merciful toward our curiosity, weakness and desires; knowing, mighty and merciful together ground the relationship.

outline.heading: He perfected everything He created
outline.gist: Ihsan is doing a thing with full care; the reflective person comes to see beauty in everything, while Satan points only at defects.

outline.heading: Opposites make blessings visible
outline.gist: Without sourness, ugliness, poverty and illness we could not value sweetness, beauty, wealth and health; a spoiled child is ungrateful while an orphan from the tents of Gaza is thankful for water.

outline.heading: Your own creation: clay, a humble fluid, then His spirit
outline.gist: From the whole cosmos the verses turn to your personal story, from clay and a lowly fluid to being shaped and given spirit.

outline.heading: Tools of connection, and how little you thank
outline.gist: Hearing, sight and understanding are what make a relationship possible; the first flaw the surah names in our side of it is ingratitude.

outline.heading: Outro

17:23.en: Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents. If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word

17:24.ar: وَٱخۡفِضۡ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ ٱلذُّلِّ مِنَ ٱلرَّحۡمَةِ وَقُل رَّبِّ ٱرۡحَمۡهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرࣰ ا
17:24.en: And lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy, and say: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little

17:25.ar: رَّبُّكُمۡ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا فِي نُفُوسِكُمۡۚ إِن تَكُونُواْ صَٰلِحِينَ فَإِنَّهُۥ كَانَ لِلۡأَوَّٰبِينَ غَفُورࣰ ا
17:25.en: Your Lord is Best Aware of what is in your minds. If ye are righteous, then lo! He was ever Forgiving unto those who turn (unto Him)

17:26.ar: وَءَاتِ ذَا ٱلۡقُرۡبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلۡمِسۡكِينَ وَٱبۡنَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ وَلَا تُبَذِّرۡ تَبۡذِيرًا
17:26.en: Give the kinsman his due, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and squander not (thy wealth) in wantonness

17:27.ar: إِنَّ ٱلۡمُبَذِّرِينَ كَانُوٓاْ إِخۡوَٰنَ ٱلشَّيَٰطِينِۖ وَكَانَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ لِرَبِّهِۦ كَفُورࣰ ا
17:27.en: Lo! the squanderers were ever brothers of the devils, and the devil was ever an ingrate to his Lord

17:28.ar: وَإِمَّا تُعۡرِضَنَّ عَنۡهُمُ ٱبۡتِغَآءَ رَحۡمَةࣲ مِّن رَّبِّكَ تَرۡجُوهَا فَقُل لَّهُمۡ قَوۡلࣰ ا مَّيۡسُورࣰ ا
17:28.en: But if thou turn away from them, seeking mercy from thy Lord, for which thou hopest, then speak unto them a reasonable word

17:29.ar: وَلَا تَجۡعَلۡ يَدَكَ مَغۡلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ وَلَا تَبۡسُطۡهَا كُلَّ ٱلۡبَسۡطِ فَتَقۡعُدَ مَلُومࣰ ا مَّحۡسُورًا
17:29.en: And let not thy hand be chained to thy neck nor open it with a complete opening, lest thou sit down rebuked, denuded

17:30.ar: إِنَّ رَبَّكَ يَبۡسُطُ ٱلرِّزۡقَ لِمَن يَشَآءُ وَيَقۡدِرُۚ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ بِعِبَادِهِۦ خَبِيرَۢا بَصِيرࣰ ا
17:30.en: Lo! thy Lord enlargeth the provision for whom He will, and straiteneth (it for whom He will). Lo, He was ever Knower, Seer of His slaves

6:151.ar: ۞قُلۡ تَعَالَوۡاْ أَتۡلُ مَا حَرَّمَ رَبُّكُمۡ عَلَيۡكُمۡۖ أَلَّا تُشۡرِكُواْ بِهِۦ شَيۡـࣰٔ اۖ وَبِٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ إِحۡسَٰنࣰ اۖ وَلَا تَقۡتُلُوٓاْ أَوۡلَٰدَكُم مِّنۡ إِمۡلَٰقࣲ نَّحۡنُ نَرۡزُقُكُمۡ وَإِيَّاهُمۡۖ وَلَا تَقۡرَبُواْ ٱلۡفَوَٰحِشَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنۡهَا وَمَا بَطَنَۖ وَلَا تَقۡتُلُواْ ٱلنَّفۡسَ ٱلَّتِي حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَّا بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ وَصَّىٰكُم بِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَعۡقِلُونَ
6:151.en: Say: Come, I will recite unto you that which your Lord hath made a sacred duty for you: That ye ascribe no thing as partner unto Him and that ye do good to parents, and that ye slay not your children because of penury - We provide for you and for them - and that ye draw not nigh to lewd things whether open or concealed. And that ye slay not the life which Allah hath made sacred, save in the course of justice. This He hath command you, in order that ye may discern

6:152.ar: وَلَا تَقۡرَبُواْ مَالَ ٱلۡيَتِيمِ إِلَّا بِٱلَّتِي هِيَ أَحۡسَنُ حَتَّىٰ يَبۡلُغَ أَشُدَّهُۥۚ وَأَوۡفُواْ ٱلۡكَيۡلَ وَٱلۡمِيزَانَ بِٱلۡقِسۡطِۖ لَا نُكَلِّفُ نَفۡسًا إِلَّا وُسۡعَهَاۖ وَإِذَا قُلۡتُمۡ فَٱعۡدِلُواْ وَلَوۡ كَانَ ذَا قُرۡبَىٰۖ وَبِعَهۡدِ ٱللَّهِ أَوۡفُواْۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ وَصَّىٰكُم بِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَذَكَّرُونَ
6:152.en: And approach not the wealth of the orphan save with that which is better, till he reach maturity. Give full measure and full weight, in justice. We task not any soul beyond its scope. And if ye give your word, do justice thereunto, even though it be (against) a kinsman; and fulfil the covenant of Allah. This He commandeth you that haply ye may remember

6:153.ar: وَأَنَّ هَٰذَا صِرَٰطِي مُسۡتَقِيمࣰ ا فَٱتَّبِعُوهُۖ وَلَا تَتَّبِعُواْ ٱلسُّبُلَ فَتَفَرَّقَ بِكُمۡ عَن سَبِيلِهِۦۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ وَصَّىٰكُم بِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَتَّقُونَ
6:153.en: And (He commandeth you, saying): This is My straight path, so follow it. Follow not other ways, lest ye be parted from His way. This hath He ordained for you, that ye may ward off (evil)

FIYkWMoPSmY.title: Listening to the Divine: Al-Isra 23-39
FIYkWMoPSmY.one_line: The ten commandments of the Quran: worship Allah alone, excellence to parents, rights in wealth; and keep Gaza alive when the news cools.
FIYkWMoPSmY.summary: An early khutbah in his Listening to the Divine series on Al-Isra 23-39, the passage scholars call the ten commandments of the Quran. He sets out the premise: a khutbah exists only to bring Allah's own words closer to the listener, and since Allah spoke first, every dua is a reply; the question is whether you listened. Before the verses he raises a concern he has voiced before: the real test of a cause is how people behave once it cools in the public eye. When the bombing stops, Gaza drops out of Muslim conversation within weeks while Sudan starves. Individual breaks from the news are healthy, but the ummah's attention must not lapse, and he charges young Muslims with keeping just causes alive, reminding them that the Prophet died thirty years before the conquests he foretold and that founders rarely see their harvest. He then reads 17:23-30 slowly: worship for Allah alone, excellence to parents with not even the sound uff, the noble word, the wing of humility, the rights of relatives, the needy and the stranded in wealth that is not yours, the wasteful as siblings of the devils, and the balance between a tight fist and an open hand. Out of time, he asks them to live as though these verses were all the Quran they had.

outline.heading: Opening
Bringing Allah's words closer
outline.gist: Speakers get carried away with their own explanations, but the only purpose of the minbar is to bring the Quran closer to the listener's consciousness; for the coming weeks he will take powerful passages people already know.

outline.heading: He spoke first; your dua is a reply
outline.gist: Listen for the words Allah chose, not the rhythm or the beautiful voice. Allah does not answer back when you speak because He already spoke; did you listen to Him, or do you only want Him to listen to you and offer a compromise?

outline.heading: The real test of a cause
outline.gist: How people behave once a cause cools down in the public eye is the true measure of their dedication; he has raised this before.

outline.heading: Gaza vanishes within weeks; Sudan starves
outline.gist: While the bombing lasts it is the only topic; three or four weeks after it stops it leaves public consciousness, as if things were back to normal, while Sudan starves. We get tired and want a break.

outline.heading: A personal break, not collective forgetting
outline.gist: Turning off the news to focus inward is healthy and prevents burnout, but it must not become the ummah's way of waiting for the issue to end. He charges his younger brothers and sisters to keep just causes alive for their generation.

outline.heading: Are the people of Gaza not tired?
outline.gist: Ignoring it until the bombing starts again is rinse and repeat; those under dictatorships do not get to tire of oppression. Change never comes quickly; it takes a generation or more, but it comes.

outline.heading: You don't have to be there for the fireworks
outline.gist: The Prophet died some thirty years before what his ummah became; Allah took him early to teach that you plant the seeds and dedicate your short time, as the founders of most movements in history never saw the result.

outline.heading: He promised Kisra's treasures to frightened people
outline.gist: In the midst of their suffering he promised the treasures of Kisra, the gates of al-Mada'in and the Roman castles, to people who could not even relieve themselves safely. He knew how change works; we heat up and cool down too fast.

outline.heading: The ten commandments of the Quran
outline.gist: These verses and the parallel passage in Al-An'am are called the Quran's ten commandments, as the Torah had its own; earlier scholars said everything of good in this world is placed in them.

outline.heading: Your Lord has decreed
outline.gist: He chooses passages scholars singled out. At his first lesson on these verses the teacher recited the opening words and spent the whole session on them: a decree is a judge's verdict.

outline.heading: Take it or leave it: His decree
outline.gist: People may say and do what they want, but this is His decision; a heart that knows the Almighty stops there and accepts whatever comes next. Your service and worship are for no one but Him.

outline.heading: None worthy but Him; then your parents
outline.gist: No one else can be seen as worthy of your worship; everyone is a distant second, a creation like you. Then comes excellence to both parents, especially if you live to see them grow old.

outline.heading: Not even uff
outline.gist: Once you have the upper hand and they are the ones in need, do not let even the sound of frustration out; you may feel it, just do not show it. Uff is not a word, only a sound built on the weakest letter.

outline.heading: Do not rebuke them; speak a noble word
outline.gist: Fa is the only Arabic letter with all five categories of weakness and none of strength. Do not chastise them for old mistakes you have not let go of; say something noble, because this is about your commitment to God.

outline.heading: No good for your parents, no good in you
outline.gist: Worship Him alone, and second, show your parents excellence; if you cannot care for those who cared for you, no amount of volunteering shows any good in you.

outline.heading: Lower the wing of humility
outline.gist: How will you worship the One who created you from nothing if you neglect those who fed and clothed you? Lower the wing of humility out of mercy; it is His decree and the speaker's job is only to convey it.

outline.heading: Have mercy on them as they raised me
outline.gist: The dua for parents; the verse speaks of parents who cared for you as a child, not those who abandoned you, and that is the majority of stories.

outline.heading: Your Lord knows what is in your hearts
outline.gist: You may feel mistreated or carry pain; He knows what happened. Do not worry about that piece, behave rightly, and He forgives those who keep returning.

outline.heading: The rights of relatives, the needy and the stranded
outline.gist: They have rights upon you, not by his opinion but by the Quran, because you owe Allah: you do not own the money, He does.

outline.heading: The wasteful are siblings of the devils
outline.gist: Do not waste what you were given. Shaytan's defining fault was ingratitude: lifted from the earth to live among the angels, he still refused to prostrate to Adam.

outline.heading: If you must leave them
outline.gist: If you have nothing to give, or must leave your parents and relatives behind to study, work or flee oppression in pursuit of your Lord's mercy, you cannot stay to serve them.

outline.heading: Neither a tight fist nor an open hand
outline.gist: Leave with kind words. Do not chain your hand to your neck or open it completely, or you will be blamed for hoarding or for waste and left with remorse.

outline.heading: Allah extends and restricts provision
outline.gist: He gives some abundance and holds back from others, and He knows His servants best. Out of time, he asks them to read the rest of the commands, which are profound.

outline.heading: As if these were your only verses
outline.gist: Imagine accepting Islam in Makkah, learning only these verses before being driven back to your tribe with Quraysh after you; living by them through verse 39 would be enough to live righteously.

outline.heading: Outro
